title: CUDA Graph handoff & energy-envelope scan — Nsight session notes
body:
Summary:

Short notes from an Nsight Systems + Nsight Compute focused scan to understand an odd interaction we observed when switching to CUDA Graph capture/replay for decoder-only workloads: end-to-end latency regressions on smaller microbatch sizes despite higher reported SM occupancy in some traces. The goal was to determine whether power/clock throttling, DMA/prefetch alignment, or kernel handoff timing in CUDA graph replay is introducing serialization pockets that drive tail-latency.

Context and hypothesis:
- Repro: 8B decoder model, single-GPU, microbatch=1..8, using CUDA Graph capture of per-token decoding kernels (attention, ff, gelu) + async memcpy prefetch.
- Observed: when moving from stream-based dispatch to cudaGraph capture/replay, average throughput increases but p95/p99 latency sometimes increases for microbatch<=2.
- Hypotheses: (H1) Graph replay causes tighter back-to-back kernel launches which interact with SM thermal/power governors causing short clock drops. (H2) CUDA Graph fragments coalesce async memcpy timing leading to bursts of DRAM contention and L2 thrashing. (H3) Kernel scheduling in replayed graphs amplifies kernel-level resource imbalance (e.g., decoder head imbalance) producing SM-idle tail windows.

What we ran (test harness):
- Baseline: stream dispatch with dynamic batching (existing prod harness)
- Treatment: cudaGraph capture/replay with identical kernels and same KV cache prefetch strategy
- Traces collected: Nsight Systems timeline (5s traces, repeat x10), Nsight Compute (top 5 kernels), nvidia-smi sampling (power/clk), custom telemetry: per-token latency histogram + NVTX markers around cudaGraphLaunch and host-side memcpy.

Key timeline observations (Nsight Systems):
- Replayed graph runs show much denser kernel clusters; gaps between kernel clusters are shorter but not zero. Several traces show short (~200-700us) gaps with near-zero SM active cycles.
- nvidia-smi samples aligned to these gaps show 10–30MHz drops in SM clock during the gap window on some runs (coarse sampling).
- Async memcpy events in some graphs appear batched at the end of a capture window instead of streaming incrementally; these coalesced memcpy bursts align with reduced L2 hit rate and elevated L2_read throughput in subsequent kernels.

Nsight Compute kernel-level findings (aggregate across top kernels):
- Effective occupancy reported by Nsight Compute: attention kernel: 36–42% (low compared to theoretical 100% for our block config)
- Warp efficiency: 78–92% depending on seq_len and microbatch. Lower warp efficiency correlates with traces that show higher tail latency.
- DRAM utilization: some kernels hit 60–75% of sustained bandwidth; when preceding coalesced memcpy bursts exist, DRAM utilization for the following kernel spikes and stalls_instructions increases.
- L2 cache miss/eviction events increase right after batched memcpy bursts (consistent pattern across multiple traces).

Quick numeric examples (representative trace):
- microbatch=1, capture/replay: avg latency per token = 110ms, p95 = 320ms; Nsight summary: attention occupancy 38%, sm_active_cycles ~ 0.62, l2_miss_rate +18% vs baseline.
- microbatch=4, stream dispatch: avg latency per token = 95ms, p95 = 110ms; occupancy 40%, more uniform kernel spacing.

Interpreting the results:
- The naive expectation that denser kernel packing always improves utilization is false here — the replayed graphs change the pacing of async dma and kernel handoffs, which in turn interacts with the memory subsystem and GPU power governors.
- Short gaps with SM clock drops suggest hardware power governor responses to instantaneous power envelope bursts (member: "energy envelope") triggered by memcpy bursts combined with compute bursts in the captured graph.
- Lower warp efficiency and occupancy are exacerbated when the capture groups contain heterogeneous kernel types (e.g., memcpy + attention + small linear) that have different resource footprints. Heterogeneous grouping produces transient contention leading to eviction storms and temporary SM idling.

Immediate mitigation experiments we tried (and quick outcomes):
1) Staggering memcpy: insert tiny host-side sleeps (100–300us) between memcpy calls during capture to force streaming memcpy timing. Outcome: reduces L2 thrashing in traces, lowers p95 by ~20% in the worst cases, but increases average latency slightly.
2) Split capture windows: capture smaller graphs per token segment (split attention vs ff) to avoid coalescing unrelated memcpy. Outcome: improves tail latency but increases CPU overhead and slightly reduces peak throughput.
3) Stream priority change: assign memcpy streams lower priority than compute streams so compute can preempt async copies on copy engines where supported. Outcome: mixed — on some hardware copy engines still saturate and force scheduling that manifests as memory contention.
4) Warm-up replay frequency: run short warm-up loops between replays to keep clocks hot and avoid sudden power governor reactions. Outcome: reduced observed clock-drop windows in traces; p95 improved modestly.

Longer-term remediation ideas:
- Capture-aware prefetching: change capture logic to mark memcpy boundaries and enforce distributed memcpy timing across the graph so that replay doesn't coalesce memcopies.
- Adaptive graph fragmenter: runtime that observes per-capture memory footprint and splits graph into fragments that minimize short-term power envelope spikes.
- Kernel fusion where safe: fuse small kernels to reduce heterogeneity. Requires careful correctness validation (floating point changes) and cost-benefit analysis.
- Collaborate with infra to test on different GPU SKUs and driver versions; telemetry suggests vendor power management heuristics are a big factor.

Follow-ups / next experiments planned:
- Run a controlled sweep varying: (a) capture fragment size, (b) memcpy injection delay (0/100/300/500us), (c) graph replay frequency, and (d) power/persistence mode (pstate override where available). Collect p50/p95/p99 and Nsight traces for 20 runs each.
- Add nvml power and clock traces at 100ms sampling alongside Nsight to validate clock-drop alignment more precisely.
- Re-run on a different driver series (NVIDIA 525.x vs 535.x) to check for driver-level scheduling differences.

Quick repro recipe (devs):
1) Checkout branch: serving-runtime/investigations/cuda-graph-handoff
2) Build test harness: bazel build //tools/decoding:microbatch_harness
3) Run capture: ./microbatch_harness --mode=cuda_graph --batch=1 --trace-nsight=1 --nvtx
4) Collect traces in ~/nsight_traces/ and run analyze script: python tools/trace_analysis/scan_graph_gaps.py ~/nsight_traces/*.nsys-rep

Notable caveats and open questions:
- We do not yet have definitive proof that SM clock governor changes are caused by instantaneous power envelope vs scheduled thermal management; coarse nvidia-smi sampling is suggestive but insufficient.
- Some GPUs in the fleet (older Ampere vs newer Ada) show different sensitivity — need broader sampling.
- We should avoid overfitting to one model/sequence length; plan to include 2B, 8B, and 30B-ish traces in the sweep.

Appendix: Useful Nsight commands and metrics to capture
- Nsight Systems recording: nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --sample=cpu --output=trace-name ./microbatch_harness ...
- Nsight Compute: ncu --section sm__throughput --metrics l2_read_throughput,l2_written_throughput,sm__warps_active.avg,sm__warps_launched.avg --kernel-regex "attention" ./libdecoder.so
- NVML quick sample loop (coarse): while true; do nvidia-smi --query-gpu=timestamp,pstate,clocks.sm,clocks.gr,clocks.mem,power.draw --format=csv -lms 100; done > nvml-sample.csv

Notes to self: capture more high-res perf counters (pc sampling via Nsight Compute) for the attention kernel — particularly sm__pipe_tensor_cycles_active and lts__t_sectors_residency to correlate stalls to memory subsystem behavior. Also follow-up with infra on driver/BIOS options to pin P-state or enable persistence mode on test nodes.

If anyone on eng-serving-runtime wants to replicate, ping me on Slack (#serving-runtime-profiling). I'll post the baseline trace set and a short analysis script in the linked PR.

End of notes.
